title: Concatenation and weighted sums: what each loses

what.formal: A **weighted-sum fusion** picks two constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$, fixed when the model is designed, and combines a per-object scalar $s$ (the narrow signal, one number per row) with a per-object row $r = (r_1, \dots, r_d)$ (the wide signal) by **broadcasting** the scalar: the output at column $j$ is $\alpha\, s + \beta\, r_j$. The output has the wide signal's width $d$. The constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the **weights**; a downstream linear layer may afterwards multiply the whole output by any constant it learns, but it receives only the mixture.
what.plain: Multiply each signal by a fixed number and add them. Since one signal is a single number per row, that number is spread across the row first, so the same contribution is added to every column.

what.md: **Why anyone wants a weighted sum.** It is the cheapest possible fusion: no extra columns, two extra scalars, and one arithmetic operation. When the two signals are known in advance to be comparable — say, two measurements of the same quantity — a fixed blend is a reasonable prior. The trouble is exactly that word *fixed*.

**What concatenation loses: representation share.** Concatenation preserves every value exactly, so it destroys no information. What it does not do is give the narrow signal a fair share of the representation. When a single column is joined to 200 columns, that column is 1 of 201 entries per row — under half a percent. The downstream weight matrix has one column of parameters for the structural signal against two hundred for the rule signal. Nothing forbids the layer from learning a large coefficient on that one column, but the architecture has offered it no head start and no interaction, and in a wide table a single coordinate is easy for training to neglect.

**What a fixed weighted sum loses: separability and the ratio.** This one is sharper. Once $\alpha\, s + \beta\, r_j$ has been formed, the two parts are added into one number and cannot be told apart again. Two different pairs $(s, r_j)$ can produce the same sum, and no downstream layer can recover which pair it was. Worse, the ratio between the structural contribution $\alpha\, s$ and the rule contribution $\beta\, r_j$ is set by the constants alone. A downstream linear layer multiplies the mixed number by a single learned constant $c$, which multiplies *both* contributions by $c$ — leaving their ratio exactly as it was.

The misconception worth naming: people assume a weighted sum is *more powerful* than concatenation because "you can always concatenate and then learn the weights." That gets it backwards. Concatenation followed by a learned linear layer is strictly **more** general than a fixed weighted sum, because the learned coefficients are chosen per column and may include weighting one signal at zero. A fixed weighted sum is the special case in which that choice has already been made and frozen.

**When each fails.** A weighted sum fails whenever the two signals should be weighted differently for different objects or different features — the ratio cannot depend on the input. Concatenation fails whenever the downstream layer is shallow, small, or under-trained, because in that case it will not discover the weighting that the narrow column needs; concatenation relies on something later doing the mixing.

example.md: **Example 1 — the dilution, in three steps.** Join a width-1 signal to a width-200 signal and ask how much of the result is structural.

items.md: Add the widths: $1 + 200 = 201$ columns in the fused table.
items.why: Concatenation adds widths because it places the blocks end to end; the rows are untouched.
One number out of every 201 in a row. Dividing entries, not widths, is what makes this a share rather than a count.

items.md: As a percentage that is $0.4975\%$, while the rule signal takes $200/201 = 99.5025\%$.
items.why: Note it is a hair under half a percent, not exactly half: the denominator is 201, so the naive guess of "1 in 200" overshoots slightly. That difference is small here but the principle — the share is $1/(d+1)$, not $1/d$ — is worth holding on to.

example.md: **Example 2 — a fixed weighted sum, and why training cannot rebalance it.** Take a structural scalar $s = 0.8$, one rule entry $r = 4.0$, and fixed weights $\alpha = \beta = 0.5$.

The structural part contributes $0.4$ and the rule part $2.0$ to the single number $2.4$ — the structural signal is $0.4 / 2.4 = 16.667\%$ of the mixed value. Now suppose training drives the downstream layer to multiply this number by $c = 3$.

The two contributions became $1.2$ and $6.0$. Their **ratio** is $1.2 : 6.0$, which is $1 : 5$ — exactly the $0.4 : 2.0$ we started with, because both were multiplied by the same $c = 3$. In terms of the original constants, the coefficients became $c\alpha = 1.5$ and $c\beta = 1.5$: still equal, still $50{:}50$. **Training can change the overall scale of the mixed number; it can never change the balance inside it.**

The merge is also irreversible. Choose a second pair with the same weights: $s = 2.4$ and $r = 2.4$ gives $0.5 \times 2.4 + 0.5 \times 2.4 = 1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4$ — the very same number as $(s = 0.8,\, r = 4.0)$. Two different worlds, one observable value. A downstream layer handed $2.4$ cannot say which vertex it is looking at.

Contrast with concatenation, where the two blocks stay in separate columns. There a downstream layer is free to place a coefficient of $7$ on the structural column and $0.1$ on a rule column — a ratio of $7 : 0.1 = 70 : 1$, the opposite emphasis — and may choose a different ratio for every rule column. That freedom is exactly what the weighted sum gives up.

This example uses one rule entry and one pair of fixed weights. It shows the frozen ratio and the irreversibility of the sum; it does not show how a per-object weighting would be produced, which is the subject of card 3.

quiz.q: Concatenation preserves every value exactly. What, then, does card 2 say it "loses"?

opts.md: Representation share — the narrow signal occupies only 1 of every $d+1$ entries, and no interaction between the two signals is created
opts.expl: Correct. It is not information loss; it is a loss of emphasis and of interaction. The narrow column is present but outnumbered, and a linear layer downstream reads the two blocks separately rather than combining them.

opts.md: The exact values of the narrow signal, which are rounded during concatenation
opts.expl: Concatenation performs no arithmetic on the entries, so nothing is rounded or altered. Claiming a numeric loss here misreads "share" as "precision".

opts.md: The rows of the narrow signal, because the wider signal overwrites them
opts.expl: Nothing is overwritten — concatenation widens the table, it does not truncate it. The row count is unchanged and both blocks survive intact.

quiz.q: A fixed weighted-sum fusion uses weights $\alpha = 0.4$ on the structural scalar and $\beta = 0.6$ on a rule entry. The structural scalar is $s = 0.5$ and the rule entry is $r = 2.0$. What is the fused value?
quiz.hint: Form each contribution first, then add. Do not simply average the two inputs — the weights are unequal.
quiz.sol: Structural contribution: 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2. Rule contribution: 0.6 × 2.0 = 1.2. Fused value: 0.2 + 1.2 = 1.4. The structural part is 0.2/1.4 ≈ 14.3% of the mixed number — a fixed share that no downstream scaling can change, since any such scaling multiplies 0.2 and 1.2 by the same constant.

quiz.q: A weighted-sum fusion uses $\alpha = \beta = 0.5$. Training continues, updating downstream layers. Can the trained model make the structural signal count more than the rule signal inside a fused entry?

opts.md: No — a downstream layer multiplies the whole mixed number by one constant, scaling both contributions equally and leaving their ratio at $50{:}50$
opts.expl: Correct. Scaling by c sends α and β to cα and cβ together, so the ratio α : β is invariant. The 50:50 balance was decided when the constants were set, and only a change to those constants — a redesign — can move it.

opts.md: Yes — gradient descent will naturally push the structural contribution up if it helps the loss
opts.expl: Gradient descent can only move the parameters that exist. The ratio is not one of them; it was consumed at design time. Training can rescale the mixture but has no dial that adjusts the balance.

opts.md: Yes — because the two signals enter through separate columns, their weights are learned separately
opts.expl: That describes concatenation, where the blocks do occupy separate columns with separately learned weights. A weighted sum has already added the two signals into one number before any learned layer sees them.

quiz.q: Which is the more expressive design: concatenate the two signals and apply a learned linear layer, or add them with fixed weights?

opts.md: Concatenate and learn — the learned coefficients can take any value, including weighting one signal at zero, so the fixed weighted sum is a special case of it
opts.expl: Correct. Every fixed weighted sum can be reproduced by a linear layer whose coefficients happen to be that fixed pair, but the linear layer can also choose any other pair per column. More freedom, not less — the intuition that "learning a weight is the same as fixing it" hides this direction of containment.

opts.md: The fixed weighted sum — it is more general because it merges the signals
opts.expl: Merging is the opposite of generality: it discards the distinction between the two parts. A frozen pair α, β is one point in the space of choices the learned layer could make.
They coincide at exactly one setting — when the learned coefficients equal the fixed α and β. Everywhere else the learned version has options the fixed one rules out.

close: **Where this is going:** neither of the first two mechanisms lets the emphasis depend on the object. The third row of the menu does — a gate computes the emphasis per object. The next card works the broadcast case numerically, and states honestly what a gate can and cannot do.
